newsitem.title: USA: Rescuers pull 5 bodies from Arizona flood scene.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers pull 5 bodies from Arizona flood scene.

text.p: Rescuers on Friday pulled five more bodies from silt, debris and murky water, bringing to eight the number of hikers found dead after a sudden flash flood roared through a narrow canyon earlier this week.

Three people were still missing and presumed dead after flood waters cascaded through the northern Arizona canyon, overcoming the hikers with a wall of water that came crashing down on Tuesday afternoon.

Seven of the hikers were from France, and Arizona officials said one of them had left two children, aged 8 and 11, behind in a motel room. Officials have taken the children to a foster care home while trying urgently to get in touch with relatives in France.

Rescuers continued on Friday to search a large area at the confluence of Antelope Creek and Lake Powell, perching on plywood and poking through the debris with poles. Specially trained dogs and divers also were being used in the search.
"People are digging through the debris pool by hand," said Sgt. Tom Florman of the Coconino County Sheriff's Office. "It's pretty tedious work."

Florman said 55 people are combing the area to try to find additional bodies that may be buried under tons of debris and silt dumped into the area by Tuesday's flood. The remains of the hikers also may have been washed into Lake Powell, downstream from the corkscrew-shaped canyon, he said.
Another sheriff's official said it would have taken "an unbelievable effort" to have withstood the flood that roared through the area on Tuesday afternoon.
Authorities have not released the names of the 11 hikers presumed killed in the flood. One man -- a tour guide -- did make it out alive.
The 11 hikers consisted of seven people from France, two from the United States, and one each from Britain and Sweden.

The British consulate in Los Angeles identified one of the hikers as Charlotte Warmington, 24, from Claverdon, Warwickshire. The Swedish consulate in Los Angeles identified another hiker as Anders Wassenius, 22, from Uddevalla.
A spokesman for the British consulate said Warmington was a nurse and reportedly an active outdoor enthusiast.
A Swedish official said she had no additional information about Wassenius.
"It was a freak accident from what I know," said Elisabeth Kihlberg, a Swedish consulate spokeswoman. "It could have happened anywhere. It could have happened in Uddevalla."
Five of the hikers were on a tour organized by TrekAmerica. The company caters to young Europeans in their 20s.
Tour guide Francisco "Poncho" Quintana is believed to be the lone survivor. He was found battered and bruised and clinging to a cliff at the bottom of the narrow canyon.
TrekAmerica said Quintana was on his way out of the canyon when two tourists asked him to return to take their picture.
The company said Quintana took the picture and the three began making their way out of the canyon when the "flash flood hit and entered the canyon with no warning."

Authorities said Quintana tried to save the people when the water came by pressing them against a canyon wall, but the raging torrent swept all three underwater. The tour guide apparently came up three times before he was able to grab some debris and get to a canyon wall.
Quintana climbed out of the water and wedged himself into a canyon wall while the water receded.
"The fact that the guy is still alive is pretty amazing," Sgt. Florman said. "I guess it wasn't his time to go."
